name: Anchoring Bias
description: Relying too heavily on the first piece of information offered (the 'anchor') when making decisions.
real_world_example: A car dealer starts with a high price, making the final negotiated price seem like a good deal.

name: Availability Heuristic
description: Overestimating the importance or likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind.
real_world_example: Fearing airplane crashes more than car crashes because plane crashes are heavily reported in the news.

name: Bandwagon Effect
description: The tendency to do or believe things because many other people do or believe the same.
real_world_example: Adopting a new JavaScript framework simply because everyone on tech Twitter is talking about it.

name: Blind-Spot Bias
description: Recognizing the impact of biases on the judgment of others, while failing to see the impact of biases on one's own judgment.
real_world_example: Believing you are completely objective in hiring decisions while assuming other managers play favorites.

name: Choice-Supportive Bias
description: The tendency to remember one's choices as better than they actually were.
real_world_example: Justifying the purchase of an expensive Samsung Galaxy S24 by ignoring its minor bugs and exaggerating its camera features.

name: Confirmation Bias
description: The tendency to search for, interpret, focus on, and remember information in a way that confirms one's preconceptions.
real_world_example: Only reading news articles from sources that align with your existing political views.

name: Decoy Effect
description: A cognitive bias in which consumers will tend to have a specific change in preference between two options when also presented with a third option that is asymmetrically dominated.
real_world_example: A medium popcorn costs $6 and a large costs $6.50, making the large seem like a massive bargain compared to the medium.

name: Dunning-Kruger Effect
description: A cognitive bias in which people with low ability at a task overestimate their ability.
real_world_example: A beginner programmer writing their first HTML page and immediately believing they can architect a complex React enterprise application.

name: Endowment Effect
description: The tendency for people to demand much more to give up an object than they would be willing to pay to acquire it.
real_world_example: Refusing to sell your old 2007 motorcycle for market value because of your emotional attachment and the maintenance you've put into it.

name: Framing Effect
description: Drawing different conclusions from the same information, depending on how that information is presented.
real_world_example: Preferring ground beef labeled '80% lean' over beef labeled '20% fat'.

name: Fundamental Attribution Error
description: The tendency to over-emphasize personality-based explanations for behaviors observed in others while under-emphasizing situational explanations.
real_world_example: Assuming a coworker is lazy because they are late, while excusing your own lateness due to bad traffic.

name: Halo Effect
description: The tendency for positive impressions of a person, company, brand or product in one area to positively influence one's opinion or feelings in other areas.
real_world_example: Assuming a physically attractive person is also naturally kind and intelligent.

name: Hindsight Bias
description: Sometimes called the 'I-knew-it-all-along' phenomenon, the tendency to see past events as being predictable at the time those events happened.
real_world_example: Claiming you knew a tech stock was going to crash only after it actually plummets.

name: In-Group Favoritism
description: The tendency for people to give preferential treatment to others they perceive to be members of their own groups.
real_world_example: Hiring a candidate simply because they attended the same coding bootcamp or university as you.

name: Loss Aversion
description: The tendency to prefer avoiding losses to acquiring equivalent gains.
real_world_example: Feeling more pain from losing $100 than the joy of finding $100.

name: Negativity Bias
description: Psychological phenomenon by which humans have a greater recall of unpleasant memories compared with positive memories.
real_world_example: Remembering a single insult from a performance review while forgetting five compliments.

name: Optimism Bias
description: The tendency to be over-optimistic, overestimating favorable and pleasing outcomes.
real_world_example: Estimating a home DIY repair will only take one hour, when it historically always takes you an entire weekend.

name: Ostrich Effect
description: Avoiding exposing oneself to information that one fears may cause psychological discomfort.
real_world_example: Refusing to look at your bank account balance after making several large, impulsive purchases.

name: Placebo Effect
description: When simply believing that something will have a certain effect on you causes it to have that effect.
real_world_example: Feeling physically energized after drinking decaf coffee because you thought it was regular coffee.

name: Self-Serving Bias
description: The tendency to claim more responsibility for successes than failures.
real_world_example: Attributing a successful project launch to your brilliant code, but blaming server issues for a failed deployment.

name: Status Quo Bias
description: The tendency to like things to stay relatively the same, perceiving any change from the baseline as a loss.
real_world_example: Continuing to use outdated legacy software (like Subversion) instead of migrating to Git simply because it's what you're used to.

name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
description: The tendency to continue an endeavor once an investment in money, effort, or time has been made, rather than cut losses.
real_world_example: Finishing a terrible book just because you're already halfway through it.

name: Survivorship Bias
description: Concentrating on the people or things that 'survived' some process and inadvertently overlooking those that didn't because of their lack of visibility.
real_world_example: Assuming starting a tech company is easy because you only hear about the successful startups and not the 90% that failed.
